title: The whole earth is family
hookLine: a jackal quotes a beautiful line to a deer, and what vasudhaiva kutumbakam really asks of a heart
carry: the wide heart counts the whole earth as family
tomorrow: why would anyone chant a verse with every word pulled apart?
last: THE LORD OF THE WORLD COMES OUT TO EVERYONE.

lines: THE CROW SAYS: YOU DON'T KNOW HIM.
cards: In the Hitopadesha, a book of fables, a jackal spots a young deer and wants him for dinner. So he asks to be the deer's friend. The deer's old friend, a crow, objects: you don't even know this one.
And the jackal answers with a beautiful line. This one is mine, that one's a stranger: that's how small hearts count. For the generous, the whole earth is family.
Vasudhaiva kutumbakam. The deer lets him in. The crow, it turns out, was right to worry.

teach.b: Undo the join first. Vasudha is the earth. Eva means indeed.
When a long a meets an e, they don't sit side by side; they fold into ai. Vasudhaiva: the earth, indeed. Kutumbakam: a household, a family.
The line isn't only the jackal's. It stands in the Maha Upanishad too, describing the generous heart. It isn't saying everyone is the same.

teach.h: SMALL HEARTS COUNT MINE AND STRANGER.
teach.b: It's saying who you count as yours depends on how wide your heart is.
And many teachers draw one more thing from the fable: a wide heart still keeps its eyes open. The deer's mistake wasn't generosity. It was not listening to an old friend.
A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.

In the Bible, the apostle Paul tells the people of Athens that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." Both lines refuse to stop the family at the edge of a tribe.
The honest difference: Paul starts from where people come from, one blood, one maker.

teach.h: THE WIDE HEART COUNTS THE WHOLE EARTH AS FAMILY.
teach.b: The Sanskrit verse starts from the one doing the counting, and how wide that person's heart is. One looks back to an origin. The other looks out from the heart.

how: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam is quoted by Hindus at weddings, in speeches and on public buildings in India, usually in its short form; the full verse contrasts the narrow-hearted and the generous.

o: how one word is borrowed into another language
how a long verse is shortened into a slogan
how two vowels fold together where words meet

games.q: one family, two ways of saying it — tap the pairs.
p: of one blood all nations of men

s: vasudhaiva kutumbakam says all religions are the same
it says the generous count the whole earth as family. that widens the family; it doesn't erase differences.
a long a and an e fold into ai
the line is only a modern slogan
it's in the Maha Upanishad, and in the Hitopadesha a jackal quotes it to a deer.

games.q: your cousin says vasudhaiva kutumbakam means every religion teaches the same thing. what's a fairer reading of the verse?
o: it's about who you count as yours: generous hearts count the whole earth.
he's right: the line teaches that all religions are identical.
it's only about blood relatives, the household at home.
games.why: the full verse sets the narrow-hearted, who count 'mine' and 'stranger', against the generous, for whom the earth is family. it widens the family without erasing differences.

practice: Think of the group chat you call family, and who's in it. Now count on your fingers the people who treated you like family without having to: a neighbor, a teacher, a friend's parent, a stranger on a hard day.
For each one, one slow breath, and a quiet thank-you.

wordCard.voice: Sandhi plainly: today, a long a and an e folding into ai, in vasudhaiva, the earth indeed.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam, the earth indeed is family; vasudhā + eva, joined.

carryVoice: Something to keep: the wide heart counts the whole earth as family, with its eyes open. Until tomorrow.
